item.title: Why are Britain's streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them | George Monbiot
item.description:
The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice

This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.

This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

item.description:
Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old

Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the midterms in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering documentary and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.

And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is winding down production. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk tweeted on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)

item.title: Even Erdoğan backs the release of Turkey’s brightest opposition leader. So why is he still in jail? | Kaya Genç
item.description:
Selahattin Demirtaş lit up the Turkish left in 2014, but was imprisoned for ‘terrorist propaganda’. His freedom would mark a new political era

A decade and a half ago, a promising figure emerged on Turkey’s political scene: Selahattin Demirtaş. A tall, talented, human rights lawyer then still in his 30s, a founder of Amnesty’s Diyarbakır branch in eastern Turkey, he was adept at thinking on his feet. And could he talk. His witty satirical speeches, broadcast on the evening news, annoyed Turkey’s establishment politicians on the right and left alike.

Demirtaş’s meteoric rise began in 2010, when he became the chair of Turkey’s main pro-Kurdish party, the Peace and Democracy party (BDP). I voted for Demirtaş in the 2014 presidential election, when he was 41. Despite his loss to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Demirtaş’s 9.7% vote share cheered up leftists such as me on what promised to be another sad election night. I voted for Demirtaş’s party again (since renamed the Peoples’ Democratic party, HDP) in the 2015 elections. That was a night to remember. Erdoğan’s Justice and Development party (AKP), which had governed since 2002, lost its parliamentary majority for the first time. Demirtaş and the HDP garnered 13.1% of the vote, a stunning result for an eco-socialist, feminist, pro-Kurdish movement. There was jubilation and partying in Cihangir, Istanbul’s bohemian heart. I celebrated into the wee hours alongside friends, convinced we would wake up to a new Turkey.

Kaya Genç is a novelist and essayist from Istanbul, and the author of The Lion and the Nightingale: A Journey Through Modern Turkey

item.title: The Booker prize winner described a dystopian Britain. But haven’t we been living in that since Brexit? | Zoe Williams
item.description:
It didn’t need a novel: even Leave voters understand the damage that has been done, as does the PM. Now all he has to do is persuade his party

Earlier this week, some people on the radio were talking about a very British dystopia. The government had disintegrated, but everyone was carrying on pretty much as they had before. Britain was isolated on the world stage and people missed Europe like hell, but weren’t allowed to visit, let alone live there.

I thought the radio people were discussing Britain post-Brexit, circa 2022. In fact, they were talking about the plot of the Booker prize-winning novel The End of Everything. Its author, M John Harrison, is renowned now for being, at 81, the oldest winner of the award, as well as the first science fiction writer to win it. But let’s also carve out a space for him on the podium of dystopian fiction, as a writer who can describe an indeterminate future in terms that are both terrifying and sound like a couple of years ago.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

item.description:
The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past

“Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize.

Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said.

item.title: Power creates wars; wars create power. But these compelling acts of storytelling are breaking the loop | Charlotte Higgins
item.description:
Artists’ acts of remembrance about destruction and violence defy the dominant narratives of heroism and sacrifice

The way stories are told about wars really matters. It is a point powerfully made by the classical scholar Alice König who, in her work on ancient and modern warfare, points out that the way war is depicted and narrativised feeds into the way wars are actually conducted. Creating and absorbing a story (whether that is told in prose or poetry, or offered by an artwork or memorial) is more than packaging or reflecting on the past; it is about generating images and expectations, and about envisioning the future. Stories, she argues, influence real-world behaviours.

The war correspondent Christina Lamb has also made this connection in relation to sexual violence in conflict: depictions of war from Homer onwards show that women have always been trafficked and raped, used as bargaining chips and spolia, their bodies made battlefields. But stories told for centuries, for millennia, have taken this violence for granted, looking blindly past the experience of women. Rape was recognised as an independent war crime and a tool of genocide only in 1998. And so it goes. Rape becomes a brutal and cheap weapon in every new war.

item.title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
item.description:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

item.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
item.description:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files.

item.title: The young rebel alliance trying to get people to love technology again
item.description:
In a spare and cavernous former eyewear emporium near the luxury stores of San Francisco’s Union Square, a motley group of tech devices is spread out across display counters and pedestals. One is a desktop computer shaped like a cartoon frog. Another is an e-ink laptop controlled by buttons made of felt. Nearby, there’s an AI assistant hidden inside a fuzzy parrot meant to perch on a user’s shoulder.

The space is like some bizarro Apple Store, but instead of offering futuristic devices you didn’t know you needed, it’s a showcase of devices you didn’t know could even exist.

This store is not a store, but a three-year-old gallery called the Intersection of Art and Technology, or TIAT, which hosts a near-constant stream of events, meetups, and exhibitions focused on experimentation among self-described creative technologists. The devices are part of TIAT’s latest group exhibition, Every Thing Computer, which explores “playful computing” and experimental interfaces.

Some are clearly one-off art projects (see the punchable oversize keyboard escape button and the computer mouse shaped like female genitalia), but others are more earnest and commercial attempts to reimagine what we want our devices to be.

Many of the people showing at TIAT, who consider themselves both artists and technologists, are building these devices as physical proof that an alternative to the current Silicon Valley ecosystem is possible. They are part of a growing community in San Francisco and beyond reconsidering how technology can bring people more joy—or at least give them more agency over the devices they use.  

“We like to call this the rebel alliance of creatives that are trying to go out and have better ideas for what the future can be,” says Liz Dorman, whose San Francisco-based startup, Era, sponsored the exhibition at TIAT. Her company is building a platform for customizable AI devices, putting her near the center of the creative technologist ecosystem.

Thanks to AI tools, more nimble factories, and the motivation of a generation who grew up with smartphones in their hands, the prospect of developing new kinds of devices is more possible, and desirable, than ever before.

“We’ve had so much lock-in and walled-garden effects because of the App Store and because of how hard it is to make hardware,” Dorman says. “That now is finally changing.”

But taking down Big Tech is beside the point for many of the people in the creative technology community. Instead of competing at the same massive scale as the tech giants, these ambitious, and predominantly young, tech people are trying to build new hardware that both serves a niche audience and broadens the spectrum of consumer technology. The more commercial among these devices are just now starting to ship, and they’re meeting the market in a moment of highly anticipated AI hardware coming from companies with trillion-dollar valuations. 

“That’s precisely why we need artists to provide perspectives on all this new technology,” says Ash Herr, TIAT’s founder.

A DIY resurgence

While there are no hard numbers on how big this scene is, there are emerging and established creative technology groups and meetups from San Francisco to New York, including TIAT, Physical Futures, Fidget Camp, Gray Area, the School for Poetic Computation, the New Museum’s New Inc., the Resonant Computing Lab, and more. Many have academic roots in vaunted computing and human-computer interface labs like Carnegie Mellon’s Human-Computer Interaction Institute, New York University’s Interactive Telecommunications Program, and several labs at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

“There are a lot of students who are kind of tired of computers,” says Marcelo Coelho, director of MIT’s Design Intelligence Lab. “In many ways, their response is to invent their own computer.”

People exploring these concepts often self-describe as creative technologists, but some see their work more broadly as indie hardware, while others find it to be closer to fashion hardware or even bespoke “couture computing.” The through line is a desire to break out of the winner-takes-all mindset that’s fueled the Big Tech companies in recent years.

“Pretty much the story of San Francisco right now is all these people with egos being like, ‘I know what the future is. Let me tell you what the future is.’ And you can’t edit or change anything,” Dorman says. “A lot of the underlying stuff that’s happening in creative tech is coming from those feelings of we actually want to take ownership over our technology.”

Dorman describes this as a shift to “couture technology,” where a more open ecosystem would allow people to customize hardware to their own specific needs. “It’s like you can sew your own shirt, or you can buy it from your favorite creative, or you can get it mass-produced,” Dorman says.

Doing it yourself is nothing new for the modern tech world, of course. Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak built the earliest version of what would become an Apple computer in a bedroom. And it’s an ethos that’s carried through the years, according to Barry Threw, executive director of Gray Area, the San Francisco-based art and technology nonprofit that’s been leading tech-centered events, education, and research programs since 2008.

“Open hardware and people wanting to have some agency and access to these kinds of tools is always a trend that’s going on,” Threw says. He points to the mid-2010s, when there was a lot of interest in DIY hardware, through events like Maker Faire, and open-source software, printed circuit boards, and microcontrollers from Arduino and Raspberry Pi.

AI has opened new opportunities for this mode of creation, with vibe coding making it vastly easier to create digital tools and applications. “It makes it more attainable for folks who start doing interesting hardware and software DIY things because the software side of it doesn’t become such a burden,” Threw says.

But AI has also spurred a related backlash, as the leading AI labs and companies pursue advancements at a pace that has even some of its own executives worried for the future of humanity. As those few big companies appear to be guiding the direction of AI’s development, nearly three-quarters of people are concerned about what they are creating. 

“When people have less confidence in the direction of their public services and institutions, not just in tech but in general, I find this DIY ethos happening,” Threw says. “They go back to trying to take some agency into their own hands and build their own tools.”

In San Francisco and other tech hubs, the concern is also personal. Software engineers, once the backbone of Silicon Valley and the tech world at large, are finding themselves replaced by the very technology they once created, sparking existential crises about what, if anything, they can do next. Creative technology is proving to be one alternative.

“Across the technology spectrum, people are searching for where meaning and value and creativity lie when it’s not possible just to be a software engineer anymore because that stuff’s getting automated,” Threw says. “As the creativity around software development has been taken over by these AI tools, hardware is kind of the next frontier.”

Creating a new creative practice

Kelin Zhang holds up a camera and takes a photo of my face on her computer screen. We’re on a video call, the pandemic-cemented default meeting mode mediated through phones or laptops with built-in cameras. The camera she’s holding, though, is not some add-on element of another device. It’s a stand-alone camera meant for taking photos. But there’s a twist: Instead of actually producing a photo, the camera uses its lens to capture and process an image and then, for reasons that are not immediately apparent, uses AI to write and print a poem about it.

Poetry Camera is Zhang’s pet project turned consumer product. Conceived on a whim with her friend Ryan Mather back in January 2023, it was willed into being through a combination of online tutorials, AI vibe coding, open-source printed circuit boards, and 3D printers. After a weekend of poking around, they built a working prototype.

“I was like, wow, it’s a lot easier to get started in hardware than I thought,” she says.

Zhang wasn’t starting from scratch. She has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from MIT, and had spent nearly a decade working in digital product design. When she had the idea for Poetry Camera, she had just left her job as staff product designer at Twitter, which had recently been acquired by Elon Musk. “I got a front-row seat to everything and I thought, You know what? I’m kind of done with corporate tech,” she says. 

ChatGPT had been released publicly just a few months earlier, and Zhang had the sense that big changes were coming to the tech world. She decided to take a year to explore what it could look like to create an AI-first digital design practice. Poetry Camera was the first thing she prototyped.

“With AI, it’s only going to get easier and easier,” Zhang says. “If you’re motivated to work on a project, it lowers the barrier by so much.”

Almost four years later, Poetry Camera is a $349 consumer product that’s garnered fans in both the tech and poetry worlds. Anthropic, a longtime supporter, put in a rush order last winter for a batch to hand out at a Super Bowl party. Poetry Camera’s success has buoyed Zhang to start a physical product studio called Tenderworld. “People are excited and delighted by form factors that aren’t just apps trapped behind the screen of a phone or a computer,” she says.

Zhang picks up the Poetry Camera she used to take my photo and rips out the receipt-like thermal paper printed with the poem it created. But instead of focusing on my face on Zhang’s screen, the camera was looking past her laptop at a shelf of other Poetry Cameras in boxes. The poem it wrote was about itself.

‘Well, I want to change it’

Like a stall at a seedy flea market, there’s a table in a storefront window near San Francisco’s Transamerica Pyramid that’s covered with dozens of random consumer technology gadgets. Spanning the past five decades, they include a Macintosh Newton tablet, several varieties of early-2000s flip phones, an alien-esque cassette tape player, an AM/FM radio shaped like a peanut M&M, and multiple garish wristwatches with built-in cameras. Nestled among these are newer devices, like the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1.

This display is part of the office of Era, the startup Dorman cofounded to build a software platform and hardware for customizable AI devices. None of the items on the table are for sale—this being San Francisco, people do pop in and ask—but rather they’re a nostalgia-tickling reminder that tech devices used to look a lot different from the rectangular phones in our pockets today. The display is a subtle prod at the bland landscape of modern hardware.

Why can’t tech look like this again?

“It hasn’t felt very optimistic recently, especially with all the releases happening by Big Tech companies,” Dorman says inside Era’s office, two 3D printers humming in the background. “It feels like these companies are not only out of touch with people, but they’re forcing technology onto people that they don’t actually want.”

Era, which has raised more than $11 million in funding, was founded to offer people the chance to decide what they want their tech to look like and how it can function, starting with the development of a puck-like AI core that it sees as the open-source basis of highly customizable devices. Calling itself “a small Gen Z team raised with smartphones,” the company is mostly twentysomethings who were still in grade school when the first iPhone was released. Dorman, who grew up in New Jersey jailbreaking the early iPhone models, was dismayed when Apple made that kind of custom hacking impossible.

Later, after an internship at Apple, she got her own job in Big Tech working for Humane, the company cofounded by former Apple executive Imran Chaudhri that raised more than $230 million to create a post-iPhone screenless AI device. That device, the AI Pin, flopped, and Dorman was not surprised. The fact that its form factor so closely resembled a police officer’s body-worn camera was one major issue, but so were more aesthetic concerns. Dorman, for one, thought there should be more variety than the single black-and-white color palette, and more of an embrace of the flexibility AI offers.

“I hated the voice and personality we chose for the device. It was the equivalent of giving everyone an iPhone and being like, you can’t change the wallpaper. And I was like, ‘Well, I want to change it,’” she says. And she did, hacking her AI Pin to use the voice of the blogger-narrator from the television teen drama Gossip Girl. She started showing off the device to her friends, and using it much more often than before. “That is very much the feeling that we’re chasing at Era.”

Dorman cofounded Era in 2025, teaming up with two other young AI-leaning technologists who were similarly concerned about the direction Big Tech and AI companies were heading.

“I think something that’s really true across the consumer landscape is everybody feels left behind by AI,” Era cofounder Megan Gole says. She previously worked at venture capital firm Sutter Hill Ventures, which was involved in OpenAI’s acquisition of former Apple design chief Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup Io in 2025. Seeing how the tech establishment envisioned AI’s rollout into mainstream culture struck her as too limited.

“Our options right now are join or die. Keep up with the AI bus or be a Luddite and get off your phone,” Gole says. Era offered a third way, built more from the ground up. “We want people’s feedback, and we want to create this new world that you guys are the center of,” she says.

Era’s intent is to provide the building blocks that make it easier for people to harness AI in their own specific and bespoke ways, breaking free from reliance on a phone to mediate its usage. The company’s puck device is envisioned as the computer inside whatever device a user wants to make, with the ability to access more than 15 different AI models and an interface that can adapt it to whatever task a user might imagine.

“Your tools can feel more retro in the sense that you know what each one is for, you use it, each interaction is meant to end, and you put it away,” Gole says.

In the AI-enabled future Era’s cofounders envision, people get to determine what, precisely, their devices are supposed to do, whether it’s a fridge magnet that delivers French cooking lessons or an e-ink display that reacts to the double-tap of a button to display the current time in Canberra, Australia.

“It enables people’s individuality to exist within an AI world that makes a very smooth median of everyone,” Gole adds.

Make hardware weird again

A few blocks away from Era’s quirky gadget collection, a different kind of AI hardware is taking shape. The much-hyped AI device from OpenAI and Io is taking final form inside the studio of LoveFrom, Ive’s closely guarded design firm. My recently planned visit to the studio was scuttled because OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was stopping by later in the day, and “everything is out,” someone at the company told me.

With Ive’s Apple design prestige and OpenAI’s market-driving muscle, many believe the forthcoming device could be the zeitgeisty iPhone of the AI age. People have reportedly taken to flying drones over LoveFrom’s studios hoping to catch a glimpse of whatever it is through now-shaded skylights.

Others are skeptical there will be a next dominant device form factor like the iPhone, or that consumers even want one to emerge.

Sebastian Bidegain and Harry Isaac‘s company, Noware, is betting there will be a market—or many markets—for much more niche tech devices. Their first product is a 128-gigabyte USB data stick, but one encased in a jewelry-inspired enclosure and glammed out with a tiny screen for customizable low-res animations. Designed to be worn as a necklace or attached as a bag charm, it’s an unexpected and flamboyant take on the banal task of carrying and sharing digital files. 

“We wanted some of the electronics in our lives to be more expressive and playful and just weird,” Isaac says.

Noware garnered enough in presales to fund production of the first batch of the device, named Puff, and its founders have managed to climb the learning curve of working with tech and jewelry manufacturers in China to actually get it built. “It’s difficult to manufacture. And that is maybe part of the reason why another bigger company hasn’t done something like this,” Bidegain says. “But I think that’s part of what makes it really cool.”

Bidegain and Isaac see barriers lowering all around, from the technology they use to design and prototype devices to the factories’ increasing ability to manufacture smaller batches of products. “For most other products there’s a range of options, and I think technology is going to be the same,” Isaac says. “I just think that the field is opening up more now that it’s becoming more accessible, and we want to be one of those options.”

Mina Fahmi also sees potential in niche tech devices. His startup, Sandbar, is building a wearable AI ring for note-taking, which sounds not all that different from the AI pins, pendants, and charms coming out from companies like Meta, Plaud, and Friend. But Sandbar’s ring, called Stream, isn’t trying to record everything. Instead, Stream is intended to be used to record specific thoughts from its wearer, who pushes a small integrated button and then whispers those thoughts directly into the ring. 

“A lot of people want to remember things without pulling out their phone,” Fahmi says.

On a recent video call, he brings his Stream ring up to his mouth and begins whispering. It’s so quiet I can’t hear him through his computer’s microphone, yet the ring picks up every word he says. It’s a way of reducing what Fahmi calls the friction of using voice to interact with technology, especially for personal thoughts or sensitive subjects. Stream, with its highly attuned microphone, is meant specifically for people to quickly record what they have in mind as easily as possible.

It’s a use case that Fahmi admits is on the fringe. There are plenty of other AI tools for capturing and summarizing conversations and work meetings, he concedes, but says not enough of them are built to help people record their own thoughts, ideas, and reflections. “We started Sandbar because we believed we would need new interfaces to fully realize the potential of AI for expanding human expression,” he says.

“We’re not out here trying to sell a million units in year one,” Fahmi adds. “What’s been clear to us is that it’s more important to create a thing that people really get value out of than to litter the earth with electronics.”

Tech gets personal

Back at TIAT’s exhibition opening, where a harpist is putting away her instrument and a DJ is setting up her decks, the crowd is thickening. Ken Kocienda stands out, and not just because he’s multiple decades older than most of the people in the room. Kocienda is arguably a member of the tech establishment that many in the exhibition are trying to rebel against. As a principal software engineer at Apple, he helped make the first iPhones, and is credited with creating its infamous keyboard autocorrect. He was also the head of product engineering at Humane.

Kocienda’s at the exhibition to see what some of the younger generations are trying to do with their technology. As someone who’s been coding since the 1980s, he’s forever curious about where software and hardware will go next, and he’s working on his own project to improve AI-assisted software development. He sees AI as opening up the potential for new forms of technology, especially special-purpose devices that run counter to the indispensable multitool approach of the iPhone. 

“I think the more personal we make technology, the more willing people are going to be to integrate it into their lives,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean Kocienda is abandoning his iPhone. “Computing paradigms don’t go away,” he says, arguing that major developments in technology build on each other while also changing the role of previous innovations. He sees a time when personally specific devices are what we primarily use, while our phones stay mostly tucked in pockets or bags, more utility than tool. “Even mainframes are still in use today,” he says.

MIT’s Coelho, who has a few students with projects in the TIAT show, says this moment of technological advancement is opening the doors to a wide range of new products and companies. “I think there’s an opportunity for thousands of startups to come up in this space,” he says.

The form these new devices will take is hard to predict, but there may be some seeds of that future in the TIAT exhibition. For TIAT founder Ash Herr, the purpose of the space is to expose more people to these emerging ideas, and to have people from across the technology and arts spectrums cross-pollinate. “I want people who are all in on their full-time tech jobs and people who are more feral to come together, learn, laugh, and ideate,” she says.

What, if anything, comes out of that is unclear. But for the creative technologists in this growing movement, the time seems ripe for offering up something new, and the tools are in their hands.

An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis, ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars.
